name: Asaiah
title: Father of Shaphan, the scribe under King Josiah
summary: Azaliah, son of Meshullam, is a biblical figure primarily known as the father of Shaphan – the royal scribe who played a decisive role during King Josiah's religious reforms in Judah. Although Azaliah does not appear as an active character in the biblical narratives, he founded one of the most influential official families in Judah's final phase. It was through his son Shaphan that the Book of the Law, discovered during temple repairs, was delivered to the king – an event that led to a profound religious and cultic reform around 622 BC. Azaliah's legacy was carried forward by his grandchildren and great-grandchildren: Ahikam, Gemariah, and Gedaliah – men who all shaped Judah's political and religious development during the dramatic period leading up to Jerusalem's fall and the Babylonian exile.
roles: ancestor of a prominent official family in Judah

keyEvents.title: Shaphan is sent to the temple
keyEvents.description: King Josiah sent Shaphan, son of Asaiah, son of Meshullam, to the temple to oversee repair work. This mission led directly to the discovery of the Book of the Law.

keyEvents.title: The Book of the Law is found and delivered
keyEvents.description: The high priest Hilkia found the Book of the Law in the house of the Lord and gave it to Shaphan, son of Asaiah. Shaphan then read the contents of the book to King Josiah.

keyEvents.title: The king's reaction to the Book of the Law
keyEvents.description: When Shaphan read the Book of the Law aloud to King Josiah, the king tore his clothes in deep grief over the people's disobedience to God's word, and this became the starting point for a comprehensive reform.

keyEvents.title: Delegation to the Prophetess Huldah
keyEvents.description: In the wake of the discovery of the Book of the Law, the king sent a delegation that included among others Ahikam, son of Shaphan and thus grandson of Azaliah, to consult the Lord through the prophetess Huldah.

keyEvents.title: The Parallel Account in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Shaphan, son of Azaliah, is also mentioned in the parallel account in 2 Chronicles, where the temple repairs and the discovery of the Book of the Law are described with some differing details.

versions.title: Father of Shaphan the Scribe
versions.reason: [minor] The title is fine, but could have been slightly more precise: "Father of Shaphan, the scribe under King Josiah" provides more context. Still retained as acceptable.; [major] The role 'leader' is not documented in the Bible for Azaliah. He is mentioned only as the father of Shaphan. There are no biblical texts assigning him a leadership role. A more appropriate role would be "father" or "ancestor," or possibly remove the role entirely.; [major] In 2 Kings 22:3, Shaphan is identified as "son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam." Thus, Azaliah's father was Meshullam, which is missing from the family data.; [major] According to 2 Kings 22:3, Azaliah's father is Meshullam (Shaphan is called "son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam"). This should be added to family.father.; [minor] In 2 Kings 22:10, it is Shaphan who reads the book to the king, and in verse 11 the king tears his clothes. Verses 12–13 concern the king sending a delegation. Including verses 12–13 under the title "Shaphan reads the Book of the Law for the king" is somewhat misleading, as this describes a different action. The description should perhaps be adjusted or the verse references narrowed.; [minor] It is Ahikam, son of Shaphan, who is sent to Huldah. Calling him "grandson of Azaliah" is a reasonable inference, but it is not explicitly stated in the text. The description should be made somewhat more cautious.; [minor] Verses 14–16 in 2 Kings 22 mention the delegation and Huldah's prophecy. Verse 14 lists the delegation, while verses 15–16 contain Huldah's response. This is accurate enough as a reference, but verse 12 mentions the actual sending and could have been included.; [minor] The summary is good, but the expression "the religious reformation" is slightly strong. "Josiah's religious reform" or "the religious reform" is more precise Norwegian wording.; [minor] In 2 Chronicles 34:8, Shaphan is mentioned as "son of Azaliah." Verses 15 and 18 mention Shaphan in connection with the discovery of the Book of the Law. Verse 16 does not mention Shaphan directly, but Shaphan delivers the book to the king in verse 18. The references are acceptable but could be tightened.

versions.summary: Azaliah, son of Meshullam, is known from the Bible as the father of Shaphan – the royal secretary who played a key role during King Josiah's religious reform in Judah. Although Azaliah himself does not appear as an active figure in the biblical accounts, he is the ancestor of one of the most influential official families in late Judah. Through his son Shaphan, the book of the law found in the temple was delivered to the king, an event that triggered a comprehensive religious reform movement. Azaliah's descendants, including Ahikam, Gemariah and Gedaliah, would shape Judah's fate all the way until the kingdom's fall and beyond.

footnotes.text: The name Azaliah (Hebrew: אֲצַלְיָהוּ, Atsalyahu) means 'YHWH has set aside/reserved'. The theophoric suffix -yahu refers to Israel's God YHWH and was very common in Judean personal names from the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, reflecting the religious culture of late Judah.

The Shaphan family developed into one of the most prominent official families in late Judah. Shaphan's sons Ahikam, Elasa, and Gemariah, as well as his grandson Gedaliah (who was appointed governor over Judah after Jerusalem's fall in 586 BCE), all held central positions during the turbulent period surrounding the kingdom's downfall.

The discovery of the Book of the Law in the temple during King Josiah's reign (around 622 BCE) has been the subject of considerable academic discussion. A wide range of scholars link this discovery to an early form of Deuteronomy, making Shaphan's role as the messenger of the text to the king of great historical and theological significance.

In archaeological excavations in the City of David in Jerusalem, bullae (clay seal impressions) with the inscription 'belonging to Gemaryahu son of Shaphan' have been found. This discovery provides strong extra-biblical confirmation of the Shaphan family's historical existence and their prominent position in late Judah.

The title 'scribe' (Hebrew: סֹפֵר, sofer) held by Shaphan denoted not only a person who wrote, but a high-ranking official at the court responsible for state administration, finances, and communication. The position can be compared to a secretary of state or chancellor in modern terms.

In rabbinic sources, the discovery of the Book of the Law under Josiah is seen as a turning point in Judah's religious history. According to tradition, King Manasseh had removed Torah scrolls from the temple during his reign, and the finding under Josiah represented a rediscovery of writings that had been actively suppressed.
